verses.text: At that time, Merodach Baladan the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a present to Hezekiah; for he heard that he had been sick, and had recovered.

Hezekiah was pleased with them, and showed them the house of his precious things, the silver, and the gold, the spices, and the precious oil, and all the house of his armor, and all that was found in his treasures. There was nothing in his house, nor in all his dominion, that Hezekiah didn’t show them.
Then Isaiah the prophet came to king Hezekiah, and asked him, “What did these men say? Where did they come from to you?” Hezekiah said, “They have come from a country far from me, even from Babylon.”
Then he asked, “What have they seen in your house?” Hezekiah answered, “They have seen all that is in my house. There is nothing among my treasures that I have not shown them.”
Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, “Hear the word of Yahweh of Armies:
‘Behold, the days are coming when all that is in your house, and that which your fathers have stored up until today, will be carried to Babylon. Nothing will be left,’ says Yahweh.
‘They will take away your sons who will issue from you, whom you shall father, and they will be eunuchs in the king of Babylon’s palace.’”
Then Hezekiah said to Isaiah, “Yahweh’s word which you have spoken is good.” He said moreover, “For there will be peace and truth in my days.”

footnotes.content: Merodach Baladan sends a gift to Hezekiah—not out of true friendship, but out of political interest. How easily we mistake attention for affection. Hezekiah has just been pulled back from death's door, and already the world is pressing close, wanting a piece of his restored fortune. We forget that humility is hardest to hold when we're most grateful to be alive.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Notice what Hezekiah shows: silver, gold, spices, precious oil, armor, treasures—everything. He keeps nothing back. Pride whispers that if we have been blessed, we should display our blessing. But there is a difference between gratitude and exhibition. Jesus later teaches that the left hand need not know what the right hand gives; here, Hezekiah displays it all, and we sense something has shifted in his heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaiah asks the hard questions. Notice how quickly the prophet arrives—as though God sends him to test not the messengers, but the king's own heart. Hezekiah's answer is direct: they come from Babylon, far away. He's accurate about the fact but seems unaware of what his openness reveals about himself. Sometimes we answer the letter of a question while missing the spirit of it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When asked what they saw, Hezekiah repeats with pride: everything. There is no hesitation, no moment where he says, 'Perhaps I shouldn't have shown them that.' Pride erases the little voice that whispers caution. The tragedy is not that Hezekiah has been blessed—it is that he cannot see how that very blessing has blinded him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaiah shifts now from questions to judgment. 'Hear the word of Yahweh of Armies'—the prophet speaks with full authority, and the tone changes. We are no longer in the realm of advice or gentle correction. The Lord has seen, and now He speaks. Sometimes love requires that we be shown the truth we cannot see ourselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All that Hezekiah has shown—all those treasures he displayed to impress the Babylonians—will one day be carried away to Babylon itself. Nothing will remain. It is not that God takes it in anger, but that God allows Hezekiah to see the consequence of his own choices made in pride. The very thing he displayed becomes the path of his downfall.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even more terrible: not just treasure, but Hezekiah's own sons will be taken and enslaved far from home. This is the cost of showing your strength to those who covet it. A king who has been restored to life now learns that restoration is not immunity. His seed will suffer for his pride. We sow, and those we love reap.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hezekiah's reply is strangely peaceful: 'Yahweh's word is good.' He accepts the judgment—not in anger, but in what we might call resignation or grace. Readers today hear an echo in this: how often do we receive hard truth more easily when it comes from someone we trust? Hezekiah does not fight the word; he simply says it is good, and finds comfort in the promise of peace during his own days. There is something about accepting what we cannot change that quiets the heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
